en: The gray-maned hero Seytek
Still bore the fault of innocence.
He pursued the cunning fugitive:
Black without and cold within,
He chased the sorcerer, saying,
“If I do not turn Kulunsur’s head,
If I do not pursue this maddened Bilgich
All the way to Beijing itself!”
“If I do not shatter his throne and game,
If I do not slaughter this hulking slave,
If I do not hew clean through his neck,
If I do not catch, devour, and butcher him,
May I sink into darkness as though never born!
They used to say that the foe who flees
Will take for his wife
The finest of black-haired beauties,
The best among all women.
But I shall spill his blood at last;
I shall seize him by the trailing hem,
And cast that accursed, doomed Bilgich
To be torn apart in the gray-wolf game.
The people will clamor in uproar,
And despair of their wrathful champion;
They will say, ‘He was born of a noble man,’
And my lineage will become known.
All forty khanates of China
Will understand and despair of life!”
So spoke brave Seytek,
Consumed by fierce intent,
Brandishing and driving with his spear.
His eyes fixed on great Bilgich,
He followed directly behind,
While the black earth, though not split in two,
Endured the pounding through its depths.
Every rise was gouged away;
Wherever the hooves struck squarely,
Trenches were carved like canals.
It became tumult, calamity, and strife,
A terror no living soul could bear.
When they entered the downward slope,
Brave Bilgich’s great Kerik
Stretched his forelegs like a deer;
When they began climbing uphill,
Kulunsur swept on like a whirlwind—
Such was the ground of their pursuit.
Amid this tale of endless tumult,
They had now drawn close
To the place established as an ambush,
Where Bilgich’s army lay concealed.
Unable to bear his wounds,
Yet still the warrior Akjoltoy
Had ridden after Seytek.
Upon the matchless Kulunsur,
He whipped him right and left,
Spurred him on from either side,
And shouted in anger,
Calling out to Khan Seytek.
Kulunsur, whom no living creature could catch,
Shot whirring like an arrow;
When he passed over black stones,
They burst apart like charcoal.
Ah, wondrous beast Kulunsur,
He flew rumbling like a cloud,
His tail streaming over his haunches,
His matchless breeding plain to see.
From the black mountains of Kaspang,
From the mouth of Kapka-Tash,
From the heights of Dyngsha,
From the fortress no mortal had entered,
The stronghold firmly sealed,
Uncle Joltoy caught up
At the ridge of the Sentry Stone.
He tugged at his armor,
Shaking him about the head and eyes:
“You have courage but no sense;
You are a witless Seytek!
By refusing to heed advice,
Will you send Joltoy to the grave?
To a place where no man can pass,
Will you cast us upon the embers?
Without even binding our hands and feet,
Will you cast us into the fire?
Alas, Seytek, may ruin take you—
My child, what if the two of us are parted?
Did I not tell you before
That the accursed Khagan
Has paths narrower than a hair
And passes even I cannot cross?
“In Beijing, where wrath cannot penetrate,
His people swarm like black beetles.
This is the great nation of China,
A place where men settle only for battle,
Where your first forefather led the charge
And the land sucked dry all who fought.
There, parted from his lions,
Your first forefather met his end.
It is no cheap land like an open ridge,
Nor is Bilgich a common warrior.
If we go any farther,
There are iron-walled enclosures
And deeply excavated pits.
There are armies of that madman,
So dense the sun cannot be seen.
Anyone who falls in cannot leap back out;
Their stubborn traps are hell itself.
That senseless scourge
Commands a well-arrayed host of ten thousand.
Once locked in combat, they never retreat;
It is a radiant and exalted land,
Where the people of Chin-Machin dwell.
Their warriors butcher any who provoke them;
They are a people who ask, ‘Where is strife?’
Whenever one among them dies,
They roast and eat another.
When their giant rage possesses them,
They strike down and eat any crow they see,
And surround and devour any wild ass.
They flare up anew whenever diminished;
No living being has ever reached their root.
Though slaughter lasts for years,
Their baleful power never fades,
And no fearsome enemy has overcome them.
Seeking to contend with them,
Long ago your father, Khan Manas, died;
This is that calamitous, prolific nation.
The greatest sorcerer and schemer,
A horse-master, swift even on foot,
The one China sends forth when turmoil comes,
The great expert guarding the throne,
The strategist of the watchman khan,
The shepherd of broad Beijing,
Where even a wolf cannot slip inside—
Great Bilgich, son of Kojozhash,
Knows more than his father knew.
His fortune and skill are perfectly matched;
He will not yield to an equal foe.
He never submits to a commanding word;
Though mighty Möngübö came swarming,
Even rebellious giants could not defeat him,
And he never yielded his measure to anyone.
Will he not lure you onward by feigning flight?
Will he not deliver you to his champions?
If you encounter them, those champions will spill blood;
When enraged, they will cleave you into a thousand pieces.
Once roused, will they not slaughter you
And bring about your death?
You gathered booty from every land
And loaded it upon the swift camel;
At one time or another,
You have made us suffer for your deeds.
Does not every man die from a single shot?
Does not this soul endure hardship?
You are a foolish man;
By refusing all human counsel,
Will you plunge your uncle,
The valiant Joltoy, into misery?”
As Uncle Joltoy spoke these words,
Kulunsur raced up beside him;
When that swift Kulunsur
Had drawn a bridle’s length ahead,
Your uncle Akjoltoy
Seized him by the cheek strap.
His bellow split heads,
His shout shattered stones;
His charger caught up in a pounding gallop,
And he rebuked brave Seytek,
Revealing countless truths,
And telling how one may die before one’s destined hour,
He made him understand life’s preciousness.
He revived the life
Of the sobbing Seytek, who had been near death.
Declaring his authority as guardian,
He pulled him back toward home.
Seytek, growing angry and impassioned, said:
“Ah, my uncle Akjoltoy,
A brave man may indeed be reckless;
When young and drinking liquor,
His mind is thin and he is drunk.
But does a man turn back from death?
Can anyone retreat from his appointed doom?
A valiant man, a heroic man,
Without contending for land or tending a people—
Let such a living soul sink into the earth,
For does not every soul die in the end?
Feeding in hollows and passing his days,
Even the most cowardly creature
Still lives out its allotted time,
But its days pass in fear,
And even a sheep dies among the reeds.
For honor and for dignity,
Does not a heroic youth die?”
So spoke brave Seytek,
Arguing grandly before calming down.
Having gained knowledge through the prize,
He obeyed Akjoltoy,
For Akjoltoy was his appointed guardian;
They separated out and took the horses,
Then turned back and took the road,
Coming at last to camp in Talas.
Riding colts and flying hunting birds,
They ranged the hillsides and hunted deer,
Lived at ease without disquiet,
Played bagalak and raised the dust,
And made broad Talas their summer pasture.
He broke the raiders’ strength,
And set his kinsmen’s hearts at rest;
He kept Talas and made it his land,
A lion of surpassing fortune,
And there he remained.
Let us leave that matter there
And begin the news from elsewhere:
At the edge of Great Beijing,
In a wondrous planted garden,
Upon the throne of great Kite—
Kite’s throne was like this:
A tower raised for pleasure.
Ask not of that tower—
A grove of plane trees surrounded it,
And at its center stood a golden throne.
Before the golden throne,
Upon a mound adorned with jewels,
On a platform built for repose,
Stood a white pavilion with jeweled pillars;
There great Kite lay.
His blue-steel weapon hung at his side,
And a blue-collared robe covered him.
His outstretched legs would not draw in,
His closed eyes would not open;
For many days and many nights
His snoring never ceased.
Unwearyingly he occupied the throne,
Doing entirely as he pleased.
When the pale dawn broke,
And wind moved through the valley,
When stars scattered from the sky
And the earth opened in glimmering light,
As though some man would come bearing news,
Then Kite’s
Snoring subsided,
His eyes opened from sleep,
His outstretched legs drew in,
And his heart heaved in turmoil.
He put on his battle gear,
Set his battle-axe in readiness,
And prepared himself for the hearth of war:
“What has happened to the black ridge
Stretching straight across the pass?
What has happened upon the heights where they camped,
What has happened to the people?”
He was the master of the land and nation,
The giant champion of Beijing,
The khan of its tribal people,
The mainstay within their nest.
The moon had waned and the year rolled on;
“Oh, my child, how many days have passed since then!
The might of one champion
